title: Binding Loader — pattern matching and selection
description: Byte-equivalent semantics for BindingLoader.load's `pattern` argument across Python / TypeScript / Rust. Two case kinds: `match` asserts the pure name matcher, and `select` asserts how `pattern` composes with `recursive` over a directory tree. There is no `validate` kind: as of 0.12.0 every string is a valid pattern and the loader never raises on one for syntactic reasons, matching apcore 0.31.0's Algorithm A25 requirement 2. Harness convention for `select`: materialize each entry of `input.files` under a temp root, creating parent directories as needed; an entry that is a strict path prefix of another entry is therefore a DIRECTORY, not a file, and must never appear in `expected.selected` (see case 034). Paths in both `files` and `selected` use '/' separators and are relative to that root; compare against the loader's results after making them relative and normalizing separators. The normative matching algorithm is specified in docs/features/binding-loader.md#normative-matching-algorithm. Tracking issue: aiperceivable/apcore-toolkit#18. Cases carrying `requires: "symlinks"` need symlink creation; a harness on a platform where that fails (unprivileged Windows) should SKIP them with a visible message, never silently pass them.

test_cases.description: An empty pattern is a VALID pattern that matches only the empty string, so it selects nothing. It is not an error.
test_cases.notes: Was a `validate` case asserting rejection until 0.12.0. apcore 0.31.0's A25 requirement 2 makes every string a valid pattern and forbids raising on one for syntactic reasons (PROTOCOL_SPEC §5.12.6 clause 6), so the loader now matches instead of refusing.

test_cases.description: `/` is an ordinary literal under A25, and a filename cannot contain one, so a pattern carrying one matches nothing. Previously rejected.

`**/` is the shape a caller reaches for first when they want recursion, and it matches nothing: the two stars collapse and the `/` is a literal no filename contains. Depth is `recursive`'s job, not the pattern's.
test_cases.notes: This case previously asserted a `path_separator` rejection, which was a genuinely useful diagnostic. A25 requirement 2 forbids it, so the diagnostic moved to documentation and the behaviour is now a silent empty result — the same answer apcore gives. Consistency with the shared config key won over the better error message; see docs/features/binding-loader.md#every-string-is-a-valid-pattern.

test_cases.description: A25 requirement 4 names `\` a literal. On a filesystem where a filename may contain a backslash, a pattern carrying one MATCHES — it is not a path separator and not a syntax error.
test_cases.notes: The discriminating case for the 0.12.0 change: an implementation still treating `\` as a separator rejects this pattern outright and cannot reach a match at all.

test_cases.description: A trailing `/` is a literal, and no filename ends with one. Previously rejected.
The canonical default matches an ordinary binding file
A different extension does not match the default
`*` crosses `.` — it is not a shell path-segment wildcard
`*` matches zero characters, so the bare suffix matches
Dotfiles are matched normally — unlike a shell glob, and preserving pre-0.12.0 behaviour in all three SDKs
A prefix-anchored pattern — the case apcore's own Rust and TypeScript loaders get wrong
A name failing the literal prefix does not match, even though the suffix does
A star in the middle with literals on both sides
Two stars backtrack correctly
Two stars still require the literal between them
`**` without a separator is just `*`; it is not globstar
`?` matches exactly one character
`?` does not match zero characters
`?` does not match two characters
`?` matches a literal dot like any other character
Character classes are NOT supported — brackets are literal. Python's Path.glob would treat this as a class; the shared matcher must not.
A file literally named with brackets matches the literal pattern
Brace expansion is NOT supported — braces are literal
Matching is case-sensitive on every platform, including macOS and Windows
The literal segment is case-sensitive too
A pattern with no metacharacters is an exact-name match
A literal pattern is anchored at both ends — not a substring search
A bare `*` matches every name
Matching is over Unicode characters, not bytes — `?` consumes one character, not one UTF-8 byte
test_cases.notes: The `e` with acute in this case is NFC (U+00E9), a single code point, so `?` matches it. Under the spec's no-normalization rule the NFD spelling (e + U+0301) would be two code points and MUST expect false. Do not let a formatter normalize this file: the case's meaning lives in its bytes.

test_cases.description: A pattern with no leading star is anchored at the start — the divergence apcore's Rust loader introduces by stripping a leading `*` and suffix-matching
Non-recursive selection with the default pattern ignores subdirectories entirely
Recursive selection matches file names at every depth without the caller writing `**/`
A non-default pattern selects a different set — the case that could not be expressed before 0.12.0
`pattern` still matches names only when `recursive` is on — a directory named to look like a match is not selected
Selected files are sorted lexicographically by path; `pattern` does not change ordering
A directory where nothing matches yields an empty list, not an error — unchanged from the pre-0.12.0 contract

A directory whose name matches is skipped in NON-recursive mode too. Case 034 pins this only for recursive traversal; without this twin, an implementation that filters on name alone selects the directory and then dies at read time with EISDIR, while one that guards on file type returns cleanly - a live three-way divergence.

`?` matches exactly one astral code point. TypeScript is the only one of the three SDKs that can plausibly get this wrong - indexing a string yields UTF-16 code units, so a naive implementation needs two `?` here.
The converse of 038: two `?` must NOT match a single astral code point. 038 alone still passes an implementation that is wrong in the other direction; the pair pins it.

A symlink whose name matches and whose TARGET is a regular file is selected. All three SDKs included symlinked files before the directory guard was added; a guard implemented with a non-following file-type check (Rust DirEntry::file_type, Node Dirent.isFile) silently drops them, which is a data-loss-shaped regression with no error. Test the target, not the link.

The converse of 040: a symlink whose target is a DIRECTORY is neither selected nor descended into, even when recursive. Following file symlinks must not become following directory symlinks - that is where cycles and tree-escape live. The real directory is still traversed normally, so the inner file appears exactly once, under its real path.

A dangling symlink whose NAME matches is skipped, not read. The following stat that makes 040 work fails here, and the failure must be swallowed as 'not a file' rather than escaping as an uncaught IO error. Harness note: this case's symlink target intentionally does not exist - create the link anyway, do not pre-create the target.

The recursive twin of 042, and the one that actually bites. A dangling link is not a directory, so a recursive walk classifies it as a file and yields it without a type check - Python hit exactly this and died at stat() with an uncaught FileNotFoundError. Apply the file-type guard in BOTH branches, not just the flat one.

The loader MUST NOT raise on a syntactically odd pattern. `**/*.binding.yaml` over a real tree returns an empty selection, exactly as apcore does — a pattern matching no file is not an error in itself (PROTOCOL_SPEC §5.12.6 clause 6).
test_cases.notes: Paired with case 003. 003 pins the matcher; this pins that the LOADER surfaces the empty result rather than an error, which is the half a pure-matcher case cannot see.
